item.title: Washington State Ferries report systemwide disruptions
item.dc:creator: Heather Bosch, Jake Renn
item.description: The Washington State Ferries service reported systemwide disruptions, Sunday, with several boats out of service all day.
item.content:encoded:
Troubled waters for ferry riders.

The Washington State Ferries service reported systemwide disruptions, Sunday, with several boats out of service all day.

There were no mechanical issues with the vessels. Instead, the ferry service simply lacked enough key crew members to safely operate them.

Tyler Thiery and his companion arrived at Colman Dock for a 6:50 p.m. ferry back to Bremerton, after the Seahawks game, only to find that the next sailing wasn’t until 7:45 p.m.

“I don’t have to work tomorrow, fortunately, for me. I think we’re just making the best of it,” Thiery said.

Service was disrupted after several ferry routes were reduced from two boats down to just one. Those runs included the Seattle to Bainbridge, Seattle to Bremerton, and the Mukilteo to Clinton routes.

Two of the four boats on the Anacortes to San Juan Island route were also pulled.

“We don’t take any of these cancellations lightly,” Washington State Ferries spokesman Justin Fujioka said.

Fujioka confirmed that, while the boats were mechanically fine, there weren’t enough crew members in key positions to operate the vessels safely.

“These are like the captains, mates, assistant engineers, chief engineers,” Fujioka said.

He explained that when those highly trained and credentialed workers call in sick or have a family emergency, the ferry service doesn’t have enough workers qualified to fill in for them.

Fujioka said they have started workforce development programs to grow that pool of workers. Riders, like Thiery, are eager to see that.

“I hope they mediate the issue, because I’m sure we’re not the only people who got stranded here and had no backup plan,” Thiery said.

Fujioka said the ferry service is trying to let riders know more quickly when there are delays and cancellations.

You can sign up for alerts on your smart phone or check their website.

item.title: Will Washington’s ‘millionaire tax’ drive people away? Business owners and lawmakers disagree
item.dc:creator: Linzi Sheldon
item.description: With Washington voters set to decide the fate of the state’s new millionaires tax in next month’s election, business owners, real estate agents, and lawmakers are making competing cases about whether the tax will strengthen or weaken the state’s economy.
item.content:encoded:
With Washington voters set to decide the fate of the state’s new millionaires tax in next month’s election, business owners, real estate agents, and lawmakers are making competing cases about whether the tax will strengthen or weaken the state’s economy.

Supporters say the tax is needed to help fund education, tax credits for businesses and families, and other public programs. Opponents argue it could drive entrepreneurs, investors, and employers out of Washington.

KIRO 7 spoke with people on both sides of the debate.

At Soak and Sage, a spa in Renton that employs about 20 people, owner Leslie Goeres says the state’s business climate played a role in her decision to expand outside Washington.

The company, which opened in 2024, is preparing to launch a second location in Nashville, Tennessee.

“Our overhead is significantly less,” Goeres said. “Our payroll expense is about 25% less than it is in Seattle.”

She and her family were spending more time in Nashville as she worked on plans for the second spa location there.

“We liked the atmosphere, we liked the restaurants, we liked the bars, we liked the gyms, we liked just the overall vibe of the city,” she said.

Then the millionaires tax became law.

“It was like, okay, this is actually happening,” she said. “We need to make some decisions.”

“Would you say the millionaires tax was sort of like the final straw in making this decision?” reporter Linzi Sheldon asked.

“Yeah, the final straw,” she said. “I think the B&O tax and the FMLA taxes and the overall overhead and the higher sales tax, all of those eat into revenue.”

Some real estate professionals say they are hearing similar concerns from clients.

Nelya Calev, a real estate agent with John L. Scott, told KIRO 7 that some high-income households are already exploring moves out of Washington in response to the tax.

“It’s like, let me call you because nobody wants it to be public,” Calev said.

She pointed to August data from the Northwest Multiple Listing Service for homes priced at $2 million and above.

Calev said the data shows inventory increased 28% from August 2025, closed sales fell 21%, and there were about 10 months of inventory on the market.

“That’s a lot of inventory, and that’s assuming we don’t add any more homes,” Calev said.

Supporters of the tax, like State Senator Manka Dhingra, dispute the idea that it will trigger significant job losses or departures.

“We’re joining 41 other states. We’re not an outlier,” Dhingra, a sponsor of the bill who represents the 45th legislative district on the Eastside, said. “There is always movement that happens.”

When asked whether she is concerned about business owners and job creators leaving Washington, Dhingra said companies have priorities that line up with what Washington can offer.

“They go where a lot of the talent is and where people want to live,” she said.

Dhingra said what people say and what people actually do is often very different and referenced a recent study on customer behavior over rising Netflix and Amazon subscription costs.

“When those monthly subscriptions go up, the members many often are like, well, we’re not going to pay anymore; we’re going to leave,” she said. “But what you see happen over and over again is that people don’t.”

She also argued that Washington’s current tax structure places a disproportionate burden on lower-income residents.

“The bottom line is we cannot continue to have a successful functioning state with one of the most regressive tax policies,” Dhingra said. “That is simply not doable.”

KIRO 7 obtained state projections from the campaign in support of the millionaires tax that show Washington expects to collect about $3.57 billion annually from the tax beginning in 2029. That’s even more than initially projected on the Senate Democrats’ website.

More than half of the revenue, about $2.15 billion, would go to the state’s general fund.

Other projected allocations include, in part:

  • $231 million for the Working Families Tax Credit
  • $127 million for a small business B&O tax credit
  • $200 million for local governments
  • $186 million for Fair Start for Kids
  • $466 million to replace revenue lost through the repeal of most of Senate Bill 5814 taxes on IT services and live presentations

“Why wasn’t this put to voters first?” reporter Linzi Sheldon asked Dhingra.

“That is what the Legislature’s job is, to make sure that we have a balanced budget, that we are making the tough decisions,” Dhingra said.

The issue now comes down to voters, who will decide on I-645 in November. Voting yes would repeal the tax. Voting no would keep it in place.

KIRO 7 plans to continue its election coverage by speaking with a business owner who supports the tax and believes the state needs the additional revenue.

item.title: ‘The peacemaker’: How Olympia residents fought off home invaders
item.dc:creator: Jack Bilyeu
item.description: Two people are in custody after a violent home invasion in Olympia, according to Thurston County Sheriff Derek Sanders.
item.content:encoded:
Two people are in custody after a violent home invasion in Olympia, according to Thurston County Sheriff Derek Sanders.

The victims told KIRO 7 the break-in turned into a chaotic group fight.

Authorities arrested one suspect shortly after the break-in; they caught the other later that day, just up the street.

It was a wild morning Friday along Lilly Road NE.

“I was in fight or flight,” Daniel Bonds, one of the victims, said. “It was just like, we have got to get these guys out of here. We did our best to do that and boy, they know not to come back here.”

Bonds and his roommate, Joshua Rush, told KIRO 7 they woke up to intruders in their apartment, then sprang into action and started fighting them.

“Right here is where it all was happening,” Rush said. “He was down on the ground, and I was on the ground.”

Rush and Bonds said they won the fight.

The sheriff’s office said the intruders were armed with an “edged weapon,” but Rush and Bonds told KIRO 7 they never had a chance to use it because one of their girlfriends bashed an intruder over the head with a statue of Buddha.

“This is it right here, the symbol of peace,” Bonds said, holding up the heavily damaged statue. “The peacemaker.”

They said one of the intruders was arrested while hiding in the bushes nearby.

Dash cam footage shared by the Thurston County Sheriff’s Office shows officers arresting the second suspect at a nearby gas station. He is seen trying to get away on his bicycle before multiple squad cars chase him.

Bonds and Rush said one of their friends was hit several times but will be okay.

There is no word yet on charges for the suspects.

item.title: Leavenworth looks to Oktoberfest to kick off a solid fall and winter tourism season
item.dc:creator: Heather Bosch
item.description: Nearly ten months after severe winter storms knocked out the Christmas lights in Leavenworth – and tore through the tourist town’s holiday profits – the city is kicking off Oktoberfest with renewed hope.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly ten months after severe winter storms knocked out the Christmas lights in Leavenworth – and tore through the tourist town’s holiday profits – the city is kicking off Oktoberfest with renewed hope.

The event, held over three weekends, brings in millions of tourism dollars and ranks second only to the city’s winter holiday season in economic impact.

But last December, shops, restaurants, and hotels lost business – some as much as 50 percent – when back-to-back atmospheric rivers caused damage, knocked out power, and took a chunk out of U-S 2, which is a major route into the city.

“Well, it was obviously quite a shock- you know, we’ve never had that big a storm,” said hat shop owner Kevin Rieke, who serves on the local chamber of commerce.

From his booth at the Oktoberfest event, he said some visitors had commented about the December storms.

“They hear the stories in the news, and they’re like, how did you guys fare? And we’re like- well, we survived, but we really appreciate you coming back.”

Jane Bushnell is one of the visitors who said she was saddened by the storms but warmed by what she saw in Leavenworth, Saturday.

“They have good community, and they bounce back, and everybody is super positive. I don’t think we’ve seen one unhappy face here this whole weekend.”

And KIRO 7 saw plenty of happy faces. “This is my first year, and vibes are good. Everyone’s so happy and friendly, said Cassidy Ogle. “We’ve just been having a blast,” said Nolen Luhan as he showed off the Bavarian-style clothing he and his friends were wearing. “We made sure we ordered our lederhosen and our dirndls.”

The smiles are encouraging to those who depend on tourism dollars.

“I know the number of ticket sales has probably exceeded previous years, so we’re back up and ready for an Oktoberfest party,” Rieke said.

Leavenworth businesses hope that momentum will carry through the holiday season.

item.title: Meet Eba, the whale-sniffing dog
item.dc:creator: Jake Chapman
item.description: As Southern Resident killer whales spend less time in Puget Sound waters, researchers are turning to an unusual member of their team to help them understand the challenges facing the endangered population: an 11-year-old rescue dog named Eba.
item.content:encoded:
As Southern Resident killer whales spend less time in Puget Sound waters, researchers are turning to an unusual member of their team for help understanding the challenges facing the endangered population: an 11-year-old rescue dog named Eba.

Researchers with SeaDoc Society say Southern Resident orcas have been largely absent from local waters this year, a troubling sign as scientists continue to monitor the population’s health.

“It’s been bad multiple years now, but really bad this year,” SeaDoc Society researcher Deborah Giles said. “That’s evidenced by the fact that we’ve hardly had the Southern Residents in the waters at all.”

Giles and fellow researcher Jim Rappold spend much of their time in the Puget Sound collecting whale feces, or scat, samples. The samples provide scientists with valuable information about the whales’ health and well-being. “It can tell us things about their nutritional status. Are they getting enough to eat? We can tell how stressed out they are,” Giles said.

Finding those samples on the open water is difficult. “I always say it’s like finding a needle in a haystack, but the haystack is moving and so is the needle and so are you,” Giles said.

That’s where Eba comes in.

The dog, rescued from the streets of Sacramento when she was about 5 months old, has been trained since 2019 to locate whale scat from aboard research vessels. According to Giles, Eba can detect samples from long distances and alert researchers to their location. “She was a rescue dog found on the streets of Sacramento as a 5-month-old puppy, and now she’s working to help save an endangered species,” Giles said.

Giles said Eba is the only dog in the world trained to perform the specialized task. “She smells them. She knows they’ve been around or they are way ahead of us,” Rappold said.

When Eba picks up a scent, Giles said the dog stops and tries to pinpoint the source. “What I think she’s trying to do is lock in on where the location is,” Giles said.

Giles said Eba took to the work almost immediately during training. “She got it right away,” Giles said. “She understood what her job was: smelling that sample and then getting to play and having to work and find the sample.”

Researchers say the information gathered from scat samples is critical to understanding the factors affecting Southern Resident killer whales, including reproductive challenges within the population.

“These feces that we collect with Eba’s help allows us to understand the massive pregnancy failure rate,” Giles said.

Scientists hope the data collected with Eba’s assistance will help guide conservation efforts and provide a clearer picture of what is needed to help the endangered whales recover

item.title: Rising above the risk: Westport breaks ground on Washington’s newest tsunami refuge
item.dc:creator: Tom Brock
item.description: The city of Westport broke ground Saturday on what will become Washington state’s latest tsunami-safe location: a new vertical evacuation tower.
item.content:encoded:
The city of Westport broke ground Saturday on what will become Washington state’s latest tsunami-safe location: a new vertical evacuation tower.

The new tower will stand on what is now a grassy field just a few hundred feet south of the Westport Marina.

Construction will involve driving large pilings into the ground to keep the structure secure against tsunami-force waves and any debris they might bring ashore.

It’s the third tsunami tower to be built in the Westport area.

The $13.7 million tower will hold about a thousand people.

Construction is scheduled to be finished by the end of next summer.

The project is getting underway after years of planning and efforts in the coastal community to improve tsunami safety.

Experts say a tsunami caused by a 9.0 magnitude earthquake in the Cascadia Subduction Zone could reach Westport within 15 minutes.

Local and state leaders broke ground on the project Saturday morning.

The new tower follows Ocosta Elementary School’s completion of the state’s first tsunami tower a decade ago, about four miles south of the new tower site.

The school district completed that tower in 2016.

Further south, near Tokeland, the Shoalwater Bay Indian Tribe built its freestanding Auntie Lee Vertical Evacuation Tower in 2022.

“This is an exciting milestone for Westport and the result of years of dedication, collaboration, and hard work,” said Danté DiSabatino, the new tower’s Project Manager for the Washington Emergency Management Division, in a released statement.

The majority of the funding comes from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. FEMA awarded the project a Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) grant in 2020.

The City of Westport provided $763,000.

Washington’s Disaster Response Account added another $763,000 in matching funds.

Construction crews will build the tower on city-owned property.

The structure will also serve as a public viewing tower.

“Westport is showing what’s possible when an entire community comes together to design and build these lifesaving tsunami vertical evacuation structures,” DiSabatino said in the statement. “There is still more work to do across Washington. In communities where natural high ground cannot be reached in time before a tsunami hits, we must build it to save lives.”

State officials say that even with the new evacuation tower, our state still needs more.

Officials used a 2025 Washington Emergency Management study of possible losses from a significant tsunami on the Washington coast to support Westport’s FEMA application.

It estimated approximately 6,075 casualties from a Cascadia Subduction Zone-created tsunami.

The study’s authors suggest additional vertical evacuation structures can provide high ground for people who may not be able to evacuate beyond the tsunami inundation zone in time.

Emergency officials say, statewide, Washington needs at least 58 vertical evacuation structures in key coastal locations to address that evacuation gap.

This story was originally published on MyNorthwest.com.

media:content.media:description: The location of the Vertical Evacuation Tower will be near the Westport Marina. It will be the third tsunami vertical evacuation structure in Washington. (Graphic courtesy Degenkolb Engineers, Rice Fergus Miller & Robert Hutchison Architects)

item.title: Lummi Nation member pleads guilty to federal charges after two bald eagles allegedly shot
item.dc:creator: MyNorthwest.Com Staff
item.description: A 39-year-old Lummi Nation member pleaded guilty Thursday to illegal firearms possession and two violations of the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act.
item.content:encoded:
A 39-year-old Lummi Nation member pleaded guilty Thursday to illegal firearms possession and two violations of the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act.

On Feb. 23, 2025, Joel David Ridley was arrested by Lummi Nation Police after reports of gunshots were made, and Ridley was found with a dead bald eagle near his SUV, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) announced.

Witness reported gunshots, saw injured eagle fall from tree

A witness on the Lummi Reservation heard the gunshot as he was walking his dog, according to records filed in the case. Walking home, the witness heard a second shot and saw a person pick up an eagle from the ground.

While the witness was on the phone with law enforcement, he saw another eagle fall from a tree on his property. The bald eagle was badly injured and was later transported to the Humane Society.

After speaking with the witness, police encountered an SUV in the area that matched the description provided by the witness. The vehicle abruptly turned into a driveway.

A records check revealed that the vehicle belonged to Ridley, and after police responded to the residence, officers observed a dead eagle in the back seat of Ridley’s vehicle.

Officers eventually spoke with Ridley in his driveway and ultimately arrested him.

A search warrant was obtained for Ridley’s vehicle, and inside it, officers found a dead eagle and a .22-caliber Savage rifle concealed between the rear seats.

The DOJ noted that Ridley is prohibited from possessing firearms due to a conviction in 2003 for first-degree assault in Whatcom County.

Both bald eagles were taken to the Washington State Humane Society in Bellingham, where it was determined they had suffered gunshot wounds. Due to the nature of the surviving bald eagle’s injuries, it was eventually euthanized.

Unlawful possession of a firearm is punishable by up to 15 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. Violating the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act is a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in prison and a $100,000 fine.

This story was originally published on MyNorthwest.com.

item.title: Point Defiance Zoo to host Thomas Dambo’s ‘Trolls’ sculptures, starts next week
item.dc:creator: KIRO 7 News Staff
item.description: Tacoma’s Point Defiance Zoo and Aquarium is set to welcome another unique family to its home.
item.content:encoded:
Tacoma’s Point Defiance Zoo and Aquarium is set to welcome another unique family to its home.

This time, instead of a member of the animal kingdom, the park will host a family of trolls.

Starting Oct. 15, Thomas Dambo’s ‘Trolls: A Field Study’ will settle in for an extended stay at both the Point Defiance Zoo and Northwest Trek Wildlife Park.

This marks the first time the trolls have been to the Pacific Northwest.

According to the Point Defiance Zoo, 12 of Danbo’s massive troll structures will be “hidden throughout the landscapes,” observing those wandering throughout the parks.

“Set among towering evergreens, winding trails, and native wildlife habitats, the exhibition transforms the Northwest scenery into a whimsical world where folklore, nature, and imagination collide,” the Point Defiance Zoo wrote on their website.

The sculptures will be at both parks until Jan. 24. Those interested in learning more about the project and purchasing tickets can visit Point Defiance Zoo’s website here.

item.title: Seahawks hold on to defeat pesky Chargers, 30-23, despite messy game
item.dc:creator: Jake Renn
item.description: The Seahawks bounce back after a tough loss in Washington to defeat the winless San Diego Chargers, 30-23.
item.content:encoded:
The Seahawks bounce back after a tough loss to Washington last week to defeat the winless San Diego Chargers, 30-23.

Down their starting running back Jadarian Price, back-up running backs Emmanuel Wilson and George Holani stepped in and stepped up.

Wilson finished the day with 81 yards and two touchdowns, while Holani finished with small, yet crucial 18 yards.

Wide receiver Rashid Shaheed also helped with the run game, picking up 33 yards, and running for a lightning-fast, 28-yard rushing touchdown.

When it came to the air, Darnold started off rough, with a strange first-play interception, just moments after the Seahawks’ defense picked off Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert -- the first time in NFL history, according to ESPN and Yahoo.

“Let’s go for three in a row next time, so we can get the ball back,” Seahawks Head Coach Mike Macdonald said in a post-game press conference.

As the game rolled along, Darnold settled in, throwing for 168 yards and two touchdowns. That being said, Darnold was sacked three times.

Macdonald noted that protecting Darnold is something they need to work on.

As for receiving, Jaxon Smith-Njigba continues to impress, catching five passes for 76 yards. The recently returned Tory Horton also caught a touchdown.

A major blow to the defense came with Leonard Williams’ departure. The experienced defensive tackle left the game early with an ankle injury.

“Doesn’t look serious right now,” Macdonald clarified.

Williams only recorded one quarterback hit in the entire game.

Despite all three sides of the team functioning well, including a strong defensive showing marked by a game-ending strip-sack by Uchenna Nwosu, seemingly endless penalties defined Sunday’s game.

Both teams combined for 30 flags -- just five short of the record the Seahawks set nearly 50 years ago against the Buccaneers.

The Seahawks will need to clean up their penalties, turnovers, and lack of quarterback protection ahead of Sunday, as the team faces the currently undefeated San Francisco 49ers.

That game is scheduled for next Sunday, Oct. 11, with kickoff slated for 1:25 p.m. at Lumen Field.

item.title: Staffing shortage forces mass schedule change for Ferries across the Sound
item.dc:creator: KIRO 7 News Staff
item.description: Staffing shortages prompted mass schedule changes, delays, and cancellations in Ferry routes across the Sound.
item.content:encoded:
In a conversation with KIRO 7 Sunday afternoon, Justin Fujioka, a Spokesperson for the Washington Department of Transportation, said staffing shortages prompted mass schedule changes, delays, and cancellations in Ferry routes across the Sound.

According to WSDOT, ferry crew members must meet Coast Guard requirements, and staffing minimums of 12-15 crew members, depending on the vessel’s size, make finding replacements when employees call out time-consuming.

Despite these shortages, the department said Sunday’s scheduling changes are not necessarily unusual but instead reflect the department’s effort to better communicate with the public when ferry routes change.

Here are the latest updates:

The #1 Chelan is in service. #2 Yakima goes out of service after the 6:20 p.m. departure from Friday Harbor to Lopez and Anacortes. The #3 Samish is out of service.

The #4 Tillikum will continue interisland service, then take additional traffic from Anacortes to Friday Harbor on the unscheduled 4:05 pm.

Canceled Sailing:

5:35 pm - Anacortes > Lopez > Friday Harbor (Westbound)

6:30 pm - Lopez > Friday Harbor (Westbound)

7:35 pm - Friday Harbor > Lopez (Eastbound)

8:15 pm - Anacortes > Lopez > Friday Harbor (Westbound)

8:20 pm - Lopez > Anacortes (Eastbound)

9:10 pm - Lopez > Friday Harbor (Westbound)

10:05 pm- Friday Harbor > Anacortes (Eastbound)

Sailing Schedule:

3:20 pm - Anacortes > Orcas > Shaw (Westbound)

4:05 pm - Anacortes > Friday Harbor Westbound) Tillikum #4

4:20 pm - Anacortes > Lopez > Friday Harbor (Westbound)

4:35 pm - Orcas > Shaw (Eastbound)

4:50 pm - Shaw > Anacortes (Eastbound)

6:05 pm - Anacortes > Shaw > Orcas (Westbound)

6:20 pm - Friday Harbor > Lopez (Eastbound)

7:05 pm - Lopez > Anacortes (Eastbound) Last trip from Lopez.

7:05 pm - Shaw > Orcas (Westbound)

7:30 pm - Orcas > Anacortes (Eastbound)

8:40 pm - All stops: Anacortes > Lopez > Shaw > Orcas > Friday Harbor (Westbound). If possible, the crew will accommodate picking up Eastbound traffic after they drop westbound traffic, and from Friday Harbor will go straight back to Anacortes.

11:00 pm - Unscheduled departure from Friday Harbor; this will be the Chelan. New reservations and changes are blocked for the day. Customers on canceled sailings will be accommodated on other departures on a first-come, first-served basis. Customers traveling on a standby basis can expect delays.

If your ferry route was changed or canceled Sunday and you choose not to take the boat, WSDOT told KIRO 7 no-show fees were waived Sunday.

Fujioka told KIRO 7 shortly before 5 pm that the department’s focus was to get at least one boat running on each route.

“We do have a schedule; our terminal employees there work really hard to kind of come up with a service plan to get as many people as possible with those two remaining vessels throughout the remainder of the night,” Fujioka said.

Number of Boats in Service/ Route:

  • Anacortes/San Juan Islands: 2 of 4 boats in service
  • Port Towsend/Coupeville: Normal service
  • Mukilteo/Clinton: 1 of 2 boats in service
  • Edmonds/Kingston: Normal service
  • Seattle/Bainbridge: 1 of 2 boats in service
  • Seattle/Bremerton: 1 of 2 boats in service
  • Fauntleroy/Vashon/Southworth: Normal service
  • Point Defiance/Tahlequah: Normal service

In addition to delays, WSDOT announced earlier Sunday afternoon that the Anacortes Ferry Terminal was experiencing an internet outage. It was unclear in our conversation with WSDOT later that evening whether the outage was still in progress. The original announcement said the outage was expected to last through Monday morning.

Fujioka told KIRO 7 that the safety of travelers is WSDOT’s top priority, but that they also understand how much cancellations and schedule changes can impact a person’s day.

“Every sailing is important, and every cancellation we know has a significant impact on at least somebody.”

item.title: How will H.R. 1 impact SNAP and other benefits for Washingtonians?
item.dc:creator: Ania Keenan
item.description: Under Senate Bill HR 1, as of October 1, more than 100,000 Washington residents may no longer be eligible for government healthcare upon reenrollment.
item.content:encoded:
Under Senate Bill HR 1, as of October 1, more than 100,000 Washington residents may no longer be eligible for government healthcare when they reenroll.

But that is not all.

According to a presentation by Carla Reyes, assistant secretary at the Washington Department of Social and Health Services, 126,000 people could lose access to the food assistance program if they fail to meet the new work requirements.

According to state data, roughly a third of people who use SNAP benefits are children.

The state has also predicted that most households that use SNAP will see a reduction in their benefits, even if they are allowed to keep some form of aid.

Under the bill, the ages at which people must keep working to maintain access to SNAP and other programs were raised by a decade to 64. Before the bill took effect, the upper limit for work requirements was 54.

The bill also requires parents with children older than 14 to return to work. Prior to the bill, exceptions for work requirements existed for veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and those 24 years old or younger. Now, those exceptions are gone.

State estimates that 3,000 or more adults in King County alone may lose access to SNAP or other food assistance benefits they relied on before the bill took effect.

One of the communities most impacted by the bill is immigrants. Under HR 1, SNAP benefits for immigrants are essentially ended for refugees, immigrants from certain countries, and people seeking asylum.

In a statement published this summer, King County noted that Non-citizen adults 19 years and older were disqualified from Apple Health, Washington State’s healthcare system, and Medicaid on Friday.

Looking ahead to the new year, the county says that by January 1, Medicaid recipients should expect their eligibility to be checked every 6 months, and retroactive coverage periods for children and pregnant people will be reduced to two months.

item.title: Morning clouds, afternoon sun Monday
item.dc:creator: Morgan Palmer
item.content:encoded:
Another morning and early afternoon of low clouds and patchy fog has given way to sunshine as a ridge of high pressure starts to weaken across the area. By no means will the end of high pressure bring active weather, though the resumption of slightly stronger onshore flow and some higher-level clouds could keep low clouds and fog from being quite as widespread by morning.

Still, we’ll have some visibility issues in spots early Monday — especially in valleys near the mountains and some parts of the South Sound. Morning lows will be in the 40s to low 50s. We’ll get some periods of sunshine Monday afternoon with highs in the upper 60s around Seattle.

The forecast through Thursday will be little-changed, with some morning clouds and afternoon sunshine and highs a little warmer than average in the mid to upper 60s.

Our next rain chance looks to arrive around Friday and linger into Saturday but there is considerable uncertainty as to the strength of the weather system, with a possibility we just have more clouds and a few isolated showers instead of a washout, but it would be our first rain chance of this month so we’ll be watching as the forecast evolves.

item.title: Organizers announce another ‘ICE Out’ to be held in Tacoma on Oct. 10
item.dc:creator: KIRO 7 News Staff
item.description: Advocates are planning another march in Tacoma next weekend calling for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to stay off the Puyallup Reservation.
item.content:encoded:
Advocates are planning another march in Tacoma next weekend calling for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to stay off the Puyallup Reservation.

The “ICE Off Our Land” march is scheduled for Saturday, Oct. 10, at 3:30 p.m. Organizers say participants will gather in a parking lot near the Puyallup Tribe Administration Building and march to the ICE detention center in Tacoma.

The demonstration will focus on tribal sovereignty and concerns about ICE’s presence on the reservation, organizers say.

The event follows a similar community-led demonstration held Saturday.

Organizers emphasized that individual Puyallup Tribal members and community members are organizing the march. It is not an official event of the Puyallup Tribe of Indians or its tribal government.

item.title: Marysville police investigate fatal crash near 10th Street and Alder Avenue
item.dc:creator: KIRO 7 News Staff
item.description: Marysville police investigated a fatal collision near the intersection of 10th Street and Alder Avenue Saturday evening.
item.content:encoded:
Marysville police investigated a fatal collision near the intersection of 10th Street and Alder Avenue Saturday evening.

Police said they closed the road for several hours while officers investigated the crash.

In an update, police said the roadway had reopened.

Police provided no other information about the crash.

item.title: 80-year-old man killed in head-on crash in Yakima County
item.dc:creator: KIRO 7 News Staff
item.description: An 80-year-old Benton City man was killed, and two others were injured in a head-on crash on Interstate 82 near Zillah Friday evening.
item.content:encoded:
An 80-year-old Benton City man was killed, and two others were injured in a head-on crash on Interstate 82 near Zillah Friday evening.

The crash happened around 5:57 p.m. at milepost 55, about three miles east of the Zillah city limits, according to Washington State Patrol.

Troopers said a 2010 Lincoln MKZ was traveling east on I-82 when it crossed the center median and struck a westbound 2019 Toyota Sienna head-on.

The driver of the Lincoln, identified by WSP as Bennie L. Crawford, died at the scene.

His passenger, an 82-year-old Benton City woman, was airlifted to Kadlec Regional Medical Center. The 36-year-old Yakima woman driving the Toyota was taken to MultiCare Yakima Memorial Hospital.

WSP listed distracted driving as the cause of the crash. The report lists whether drugs or alcohol were involved as unknown.

media:content.media:description: State patrols are searching for anyone with information about the man killed or the vehicle that hit him.
